pitfalls: LFTs bundled in a 'daily bloods' order set → change the order set as well as the rule.
Hard blocks anger clinicians → use a soft stop with a reason, not a block.
Exception groups not flagged in the LIMS → check exclusions against the EPR for a sample.
Gains fade after rotation → keep the rule, not only teaching.
pearls: Recruit the duty biochemist and a digital clinical safety officer.
Show the cost and carbon of avoidable tests per month.
Report by ward; it makes the change local.

pitfalls: Lab changes the haemolysis threshold between cycles → fix the threshold before cycle 1.
Collection method rarely documented → use a short 2-week sticker on the request to capture it.
Pneumatic tube settings are outside ED control → involve estates and the lab early.
Staff feel blamed → report by area, not by person.
pearls: Recruit the lab quality manager and an ED nurse educator.
Measure delay to a valid potassium; it shows the patient impact.
Feed back the rate monthly on the ED safety board.

pitfalls: Small numbers per month → use a 6–12 month retrospective window for cycle 1.
Pre-malignant lesions debated → list the included diagnoses with a pathologist before cycle 1.
Surgeon on leave when report arrives → auto-listing to the MDT removes the single point of failure.
Letters sent but no plan → count only actions that state what happens next.
pearls: Recruit a consultant histopathologist and an MDT coordinator.
Include specialties beyond general surgery; gynaecology and urology specimens are often forgotten.
Track the time to MDT discussion as a secondary measure.

pitfalls: Paper and electronic records both in use → audit one ward type only, or confirm every ward uses the electronic system before cycle 1.
Night-time repeats look worse because of staffing → report day and night separately so the fix is aimed correctly.
Nurses object that the alert adds noise → set the alert only for scores of 5 or more, not for every set.
A partial set (e.g. saturations only) gets counted as a repeat → define 'full set' as all seven NEWS2 parameters before cycle 1.
Gains fade when the alert is switched off after an upgrade → name the system owner who keeps the setting.
pearls: Recruit the critical care outreach lead; they already review these reports.
Pull the trigger list from the observations system; it takes minutes, not hours.
Agree what counts as 'next set' with the ward sisters before collecting.
Share each ward's result with its own sister, not just the trust total.

pitfalls: Suspected infection is not always written down → use the sepsis screen or the first antibiotic prescription as the marker, agreed before cycle 1.
Patients moved to ED resus or critical care drop out of the ward record → exclude transfers within 30 minutes and count them.
Small numbers per ward → pool all adult wards.
Staff see the re-score as a nursing task only → make the timer visible to the doctor reviewing the patient too.
pearls: Recruit the sepsis nurse or outreach team; they already hold the list of high-risk screens.
Collect time-to-antibiotics as a context field, but keep the re-score as the single measure.
Agree that the first qualifying score is time zero before starting.

pitfalls: Staff fear delaying antibiotics → state that culture must not delay the first dose beyond the NICE time limit.
Collection time on the lab system is the label print time → check a few against the notes before cycle 1.
Out-of-hours shortages of culture bottles → check stock in the grab bags as part of the fix.
Contamination rises when cultures are rushed → record contaminants so the fix does not trade one problem for another.
pearls: Recruit a microbiologist; they can pull collection times in bulk.
Pair with the pharmacy antibiotic report to find cases fast.
Keep the grab bag checklist owned by the ward sister, not the audit team.

pitfalls: Time zero is unclear when the score drifts up and down → use the first 5 or 6 with a documented infection concern, agreed before cycle 1.
Clinicians read 3 hours as a target → present the delay after decision as a second number.
Patients who never needed antibiotics get included → only include those given antibiotics.
The stat alert is ignored → route it to the nurse in charge, not a generic inbox.
pearls: Recruit an antimicrobial pharmacist; they can pull first-dose times.
Show the result as a run chart of minutes, not only a percentage.
Keep medium and high risk separate so each gets its own standard.

pitfalls: Readings taken with the wrong technique create false drops → record the standing time and exclude readings without it.
Doctors say review happened but was not written → count only written reviews and agree this before cycle 1.
Pharmacist and doctor reviews overlap → accept either, as long as a decision per drug is recorded.
The automatic task is dismissed without action → audit the notes, not the task completion log.
pearls: Recruit the ward pharmacist; they often do the review anyway.
Pull cases from the observations system rather than reading every chart.
Keep the 48-hour window; same-day is unrealistic at weekends.

pitfalls: Incident reports are completed late and by a different person → use the contemporaneous nursing note as the source.
Unwitnessed falls where the patient is already standing → record separately and exclude from the denominator.
Nurses feel audited as individuals → present by ward, never by name.
Checklist becomes one more form → replace the existing post-fall note rather than add to it.
pearls: Recruit the falls prevention nurse lead early.
Agree with the ward sisters exactly what counts as a documented check.
Put the checklist in the post-fall grab folder on each ward.

pitfalls: Paper neuro charts get lost → confirm where charts are filed before cycle 1.
Night falls with one nurse per bay → report night falls separately.
Unwitnessed falls without clear head injury inflate the denominator → apply one definition in both cycles.
Staff wake patients repeatedly and families object → explain why the first 6 hours matter; frequency drops after that.
pearls: Recruit the falls lead and a ward sister from a high-falls ward.
Use the incident system's 'head injury' tick box to find cases quickly.
Record anticoagulant use; it makes the case for the fix.

pitfalls: Patients waiting many hours in ED → decide before cycle 1 whether the clock starts at ED arrival or ward arrival, and keep it the same.
Assessments copied from the ED record → accept an ED assessment only if timed within the window.
Nurses see it as a tick box → show the ulcer incidence alongside the result.
Mandatory field filled with defaults → spot-check 5 scores against the patient's condition.
pearls: Recruit the tissue viability nurse; they often hold ward data.
EPR timestamps make this a 1-hour data pull.
Feed results back to each ward sister within a week.

pitfalls: Charts completed retrospectively at shift end → look for identical times and flag them.
Night gaps to let patients sleep → the pass criterion allows a documented clinical reason; agree this before cycle 1.
Air mattresses used as a reason not to turn → record mattress type but do not exempt.
Healthcare assistants feel blamed → present by ward and involve them in designing the alert.
pearls: Recruit a healthcare assistant champion on each ward.
Pick one fixed 24-hour window per patient to keep collection fast.
Ask the tissue viability nurse to co-present the results.

pitfalls: MUST scores calculated wrongly → check a sample of scores against weight and BMI.
Dietitian capacity worries → agree triage with the dietetic lead before switching on referrals.
Supplements prescribed but not given → record administration as a context field.
Weekend admissions miss the 48-hour window → report weekend admissions separately.
pearls: Recruit the lead dietitian; they can pull referral times.
Use the EPR MUST report to find cases.
Share results at the ward nurse huddle.

pitfalls: Delirium not written as the indication → search e-prescribing for all new antipsychotic starts in people aged 65 or over and confirm from notes.
Psychiatry liaison continued the drug → accept their documented reason and stop date as a pass.
As-required doses never given are counted → record doses given, but judge the prescription.
Default stop dates annoy prescribers → allow a one-click extension with a reason.
pearls: Recruit a ward pharmacist and a liaison psychiatrist.
Include the discharge prescription; that is where harm spreads.
Report the number still on an antipsychotic at discharge as a second figure.

pitfalls: Charts started for patients who do not need them dilute effort → audit only patients on IV fluids.
Oral intake is not recorded, so totals look low → note if oral intake is missing but still count the total.
Night staff blamed → agree who totals the chart before cycle 1.
Gains fade after the audit [9398] → build the total into the chart itself, not into reminders.
pearls: Recruit the AKI nurse specialist.
Audit on two different weekdays to avoid one bad day skewing results.
Photograph paper charts (no identifiers) to show what 'totalled' looks like.

pitfalls: Doctors and nurses disagree on what counts as valid → agree the indication list with urology and infection prevention before cycle 1.
Nurses worry about removing catheters without a doctor → the protocol must name who can remove.
Point prevalence misses short catheters → run two audit days a week apart.
Retention after removal worries staff → include a bladder scan step in the protocol.
pearls: Recruit the continence nurse and an infection prevention nurse.
A ward walk-round finds catheters faster than the EPR.
Use the catheter passport if the trust already has one.

pitfalls: Dipsticks done but not written down → ask nurses on the audit wards and record 'unknown' honestly.
Doctors worry about missing sepsis → the fix sends a culture; it does not stop treatment.
Catheter status not flagged in the EPR → the fix needs a catheter flag first.
Result improves only on the pilot ward → roll out the EPR stop trust-wide once shown to work.
pearls: Recruit an antimicrobial pharmacist and the continence nurse.
Pull cases from the lab 'catheter specimen' list.
Record antibiotic starts; the saving makes the case to managers.

pitfalls: Doctors keep cannulas 'just in case' → allow a documented reason; the aim is conscious decisions.
Oral switch not done, so cannula looks used → note IV antibiotics that could have been switched as a context finding.
Point prevalence misses short stays → use two days a week apart.
Nurses unsure they may remove cannulas → confirm the trust policy allows nurse-led removal.
pearls: Recruit the infection prevention nurse; they may already run a cannula audit.
Do the walk-round at mid-morning after drug rounds.
Show the number of idle cannula days per month; it is a striking figure.

pitfalls: Oxygen treated as 'not a drug' by staff → show the BTS wording at ward huddles.
E-prescribing lists oxygen as 'as required', so it never appears on the round → change it to scheduled with the pharmacy system team.
Patients who stopped oxygen mid-day confuse counts → count only rounds while on oxygen.
Gains fade after the audit → build it into the system, not a poster.
pearls: Recruit a respiratory nurse specialist and the e-prescribing pharmacist.
Collect device and target range as context; they show the wider picture.
Audit on two different weekdays.

pitfalls: Discussions happen but are written in a different part of the notes → check both the form and the notes.
Decisions made at night with family unreachable → a clear reason and plan counts as a pass.
Clinicians feel their judgement is being questioned → audit the record, not the decision.
Mandatory fields filled with 'N/A' → spot-check 5 forms for meaningful content.
pearls: Recruit the resuscitation officer; they hold the register.
Involve a palliative care consultant in presenting the results.
Share one anonymised good example with every audited team.

pitfalls: Weekend decisions wait until Monday → report weekday and weekend separately; agree 24 hours includes weekends.
Endorsement recorded only as a signature without a date → count undated signatures as fail and fix the form.
Consultants feel second-guessed → frame it as protecting junior colleagues.
ReSPECT and DNACPR forms coexist → include both and record which.
pearls: Recruit an acute medicine consultant as sponsor.
The resuscitation officer's register makes case-finding quick.
Present decisions changed at review; they show why endorsement matters.

pitfalls: Small numbers → use a 6-month window and report every case, not just a percentage.
Bruise mentioned only in the examination, not triage → search free text as well as codes.
Mobility not recorded → record 'not recorded' as its own category; it is a finding.
Parents' distress makes staff reluctant to refer → the triage rule removes individual judgement.
pearls: Recruit the named doctor for safeguarding children as co-lead.
Ask the ED IT lead for a free-text search of 'bruise' in under-1s.
Use the local safeguarding partnership bruising protocol for the referral steps.

pitfalls: Arrival time and administration time sit in different systems → agree before cycle 1 which timestamp counts, and use administration time only.
Patients who were never neutropenic get excluded later, changing the denominator → include all treated as suspected neutropenic sepsis and report confirmed cases separately.
ED nurses may object to a PGD they have not been trained on → agree the PGD with pharmacy and the ED nurse educator before launch.
Gains fade when the audit team rotates → hand the dashboard to the acute oncology nurse team.
pearls: Recruit the acute oncology nurse; they already see most of these patients within 24 hours.
Stock piperacillin with tazobactam in the ED resus cupboard so the dose is not delayed by pharmacy.
Ask the chemotherapy unit to give patients an alert card to show at triage.
Report median minutes as well as the percentage so small improvements are visible.

pitfalls: Local policy may still recommend gentamicin for shock or allergy → agree the local exceptions with microbiology before cycle 1 and count them as passes.
ED sepsis protocols override the oncology guideline → change the ED sepsis page at the same time.
Small numbers if few patients get gentamicin → report the count as well as the percentage.
Microbiologists may object without local resistance data → bring the latest bacteraemia sensitivity report to the meeting.
pearls: Recruit the oncology or antimicrobial pharmacist; they can check every new episode within 24 hours.
Check the penicillin-allergy regimen at the same time so the fix does not leave a gap.
Share one-page results with ED and acute medicine, where most first doses are prescribed.
Build the order set so the default is the correct regimen with one click.

pitfalls: Scores written by the medical team before neutrophils are known → count only scores recorded after the count is available.
Weekend admissions without acute oncology cover → record day of admission and report weekends separately.
Staff tick 'low risk' without a number → a pass needs the named score and its total.
The field is added but nobody acts on it → track step-down to oral antibiotics in the re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the acute oncology nurse specialist to own the field.
Print the MASCC score on the back of the neutropenic sepsis pathway so it is scored at the bedside.
Agree with consultants before cycle 1 which score counts as validated.
Link the score to a one-line step-down plan so it has a purpose.

pitfalls: Information is given but written in a place you do not search → list every document type before cycle 1 (consent form, nurse assessment, clinic letter).
Oral chemotherapy started in clinic by a different team → include oral starts and record the team.
Nurses object to another tick box → replace a free-text field rather than adding a new page.
Leaflet stock runs out → ask the unit manager to keep alert cards with the consent packs.
pearls: Recruit the chemotherapy nurse lead; they run pre-assessment.
Use the UKONS or local alert card so the helpline number is always the same.
Check oral chemotherapy clinics as well; they are often missed.
Ask two patients at the re-audit to show you their card; it makes the result real for staff.

pitfalls: Serology done at another hospital is not visible → check referral letters and record 'external result' as a pass only if the result is written.
Low numbers in a small unit → include all new starts over 6 months.
Clinicians argue that anti-HBc is not needed → quote CG165 1.5.48; prophylaxis decisions depend on it.
The hard stop is overridden → report overrides at the re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the haematology pharmacist who verifies cycle 1.
Add HBV serology to the lymphoma new-patient blood order set.
Check that positive results trigger a hepatology or virology referral as a secondary measure.
Ask pharmacy to keep the hard stop on the checklist after the audit team leaves.

pitfalls: Urgent starts before the result returns → record the documented reason and report them separately.
Result sent to a genetics portal the team cannot see → confirm where results live before cycle 1.
Oncologists may fear delays → share the laboratory turnaround time and request the test at the first clinic visit.
Variant found but dose not reduced → collect dose adjustment as a secondary field.
pearls: Recruit the oncology pharmacist; they verify every cycle 1.
Add the DPYD test to the colorectal and breast new-patient blood order sets.
Ask the laboratory for the median turnaround so clinics can plan.
Present one near-miss case at the meeting; it wins support fast.

pitfalls: Consent written after the unit started → record both times and count only discussions before the start.
Out-of-hours transfusions have poorer documentation → report in-hours and out-of-hours separately.
Juniors say it takes too long → keep the section to four tick boxes and one free-text line.
Patients without capacity are counted as fails → accept a documented best-interests decision.
pearls: Recruit the hospital transfusion practitioner; they already audit transfusion records.
Keep leaflets with the transfusion packs on each ward.
Include circulatory overload in the risk box; the 2024 national alert asks for it.
Ask the blood bank to reject e-orders with an empty consent section only after the pilot has worked.

pitfalls: The form is ticked without thought → count as a pass only if every question is answered and a mitigation is written when risk is present.
Paper forms get separated from the notes → check the transfusion record and the EPR.
Doctors object to another form → replace an existing section of the prescription rather than adding a sheet.
Gains fade after rotation → include the form in junior doctor induction and keep the transfusion practitioner's monthly spot check.
pearls: Recruit the hospital transfusion practitioner; the NatPSA already requires them to audit this.
Use the current SHOT 2024 version of the tool, which includes severe chronic anaemia.
Pair results with any local TACO incidents to show why it matters.
Ask blood bank staff to prompt when an order arrives without the assessment.

pitfalls: Symptomatic anaemia is used loosely as a reason → agree before cycle 1 what counts as a documented reason.
The pre-transfusion haemoglobin is days old → record its date and require one within 24 hours.
Consultants disagree with a single threshold in frail patients → report results by ward and invite them to the meeting.
Changing exclusions between cycles → fix the exclusion list in writing before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the transfusion practitioner and a haematology consultant to present with you.
Look at out-of-hours transfusions separately; they are more often outside threshold.
Pair the threshold with single-unit dosing on the same request screen.
Share each ward's results with its matron, not just the doctors.

pitfalls: Bleeding status is not recorded → agree to classify from nursing notes and exclude unclear cases consistently.
Haematology units use higher thresholds for fever → write these exceptions into the pass rule before cycle 1.
Laboratory staff are uneasy querying senior clinicians → give them a written script and haematology backing.
Numbers are small outside haematology → collect over a longer period rather than cutting the sample.
pearls: Recruit a haematology consultant to agree the exceptions list.
Use the blood bank issue list; it captures every unit.
Show the cost and shelf-life of platelets on the results slide.
Pair with the existing library audit on post-transfusion platelet counts for the next cycle.

pitfalls: Local policies (and some society guidance) still use a threshold of 20×10⁹/L for lines → agree the local rule with haematology and anaesthesia before cycle 1 and report counts below 20 separately.
Line insertions are poorly logged → use the blood bank issue list to find platelet units linked to procedures.
Operators may refuse without platelets → pair the change with ultrasound-guided insertion by an experienced operator.
Small numbers → extend the collection period rather than the population.
pearls: Recruit an anaesthetist who inserts lines and a haematologist who does biopsies.
Record ultrasound guidance; it reassures sceptics.
Report bleeding complications alongside compliance to show safety.
Ask ICU to join; they insert most lines in thrombocytopenic patients.

pitfalls: 'Procedure planned' but never done → record whether the procedure happened within 12 hours.
Major haemorrhage packs inflate numbers → exclude protocol activations.
ICU and liver teams may object → invite them to agree the exceptions before cycle 1.
Warfarin reversal with FFP hides the lack of PCC stock → check PCC availability as part of the fix.
pearls: Recruit the transfusion laboratory manager; they see every request.
Show the cost per unit and the TRALI/TACO risk on one slide.
Ask the on-call haematologist to log each referral for the re-audit.
Keep PCC stocked in ED so warfarin reversal never needs FFP.

pitfalls: Time of recognition is vague → use the first documented time of 'major bleed' or haemodynamic instability, agreed before cycle 1.
Few cases per month → collect retrospectively over 6–12 months and report each case.
Haematology may want to approve each dose → agree a dosing chart they sign off in advance.
Stock expires unused in ED → agree rotation with the blood bank.
pearls: Recruit the transfusion laboratory manager and an ED consultant.
Write the dosing chart on the PCC box itself.
Record IV vitamin K as a secondary field; it should be given with PCC.
Present one delayed case as a short timeline; it persuades faster than percentages.

pitfalls: Sample taken but time not recorded → use the laboratory collection time, not the report time.
Small numbers → include all cases for 6–12 months and present case by case.
Teams recheck only if still bleeding → explain that surgery and endoscopy decisions depend on it.
Changing the time window between cycles → fix the 60-minute window before cycle 1.
pearls: Collect this at the same time as the PCC timing audit; the cases are the same.
Recruit the blood bank; they can remind the ward when PCC is issued.
Report INR values as well as timing so the committee sees reversal adequacy.
Put the step on the PCC box label.

pitfalls: Paper and electronic observations are split → check both for every unit.
Night transfusions have fewer staff → report day and night separately and avoid non-urgent night transfusions.
Nurses object to alerts → agree the alert wording with ward managers.
The 15-minute window is argued over → fix it (5–25 minutes) before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the transfusion practitioner and a ward matron.
Report by ward; ward-level results drive nursing change.
Pair with a push to avoid starting non-urgent units after 20:00.
Share any reaction found late as a learning case.

pitfalls: Low attendance numbers in a DGH → collect over 12 months or pool with a neighbouring hospital.
Arrival time and triage time differ → agree which time counts before cycle 1.
ED staff may doubt pain severity → include the patient's care plan and triage pain score in the fix.
Frequent attenders dominate the sample → report per attendance and the number of individual patients.
pearls: Recruit the haemoglobinopathy specialist nurse and a patient from the local sickle cell society.
Put individual care plans on the EPR alert so triage can see the patient's usual opioid.
Report median minutes as well as the percentage.
Include children; paediatric ED often has different barriers.

pitfalls: Sedation scores recorded on a separate chart → check all charts before marking a fail.
Transfer from ED to ward breaks the schedule → include both areas and note where gaps occur.
Nurses see hourly checks as excessive → share the acute chest syndrome risk and agree a stop point at 6 hours.
Low numbers → pool 12 months of data.
pearls: Recruit the haemoglobinopathy nurse and the ward matron.
Build the schedule into the PCA chart as well.
Report the gap by hour; it shows exactly where monitoring drops.
Include respiratory rate as a secondary measure; it catches hypoventilation earlier.

pitfalls: Reassessment is done but not scored → count only numeric or age-appropriate scale scores.
Busy EDs cannot manage 30-minute checks → assign the task to the nurse giving the dose.
Patients moved between areas → track across ED and ward.
Children need age-appropriate tools → list accepted tools before cycle 1.
pearls: Run this alongside the time-to-analgesia audit; the same notes give both.
Recruit a patient representative to review the results.
Report the proportion who needed a second dose; it shows why reassessment matters.
Put the reassessment reminder on the sickle cell care plan alert.

pitfalls: Cancer status is unclear in the notes → use the NICE definition of active cancer and check oncology letters.
Oncologists prefer LMWH for some tumours → any documented reason counts as a pass.
Outpatient PE pathways are missed → include ambulatory emergency care cases.
Drug interactions with SACT are not checked → ask the oncology pharmacist to review the proforma.
pearls: Recruit the anticoagulation nurse and oncology pharmacist.
Add a short interaction list for common SACT drugs to the proforma.
Capture the 3–6 month review date at discharge for the next audit cycle.
Share results with acute oncology; they see these patients first.

pitfalls: Haematology units may have local policies adding glycopeptides → agree local indications with microbiology before cycle 1.
Glycopeptides started after 48 hours for a positive culture are appropriate → only count the first 48 hours.
Small numbers in solid tumour units → include haematology.
The order set is bypassed with free-text prescribing → check free-text orders at re-audit.
pearls: Recruit the antimicrobial pharmacist and a microbiologist.
Collect with the aminoglycoside audit; the same drug charts answer both.
Report days of glycopeptide therapy saved.
Ask the line team to record line-site signs at admission so exceptions are clear.

pitfalls: Criteria judged loosely from notes → pull temperature and NEWS2 straight from e-obs and agree the exact criteria list before cycle 1.
Senior clinicians object that the patient 'looks unwell' → accept a documented reason as a pass; count only undocumented delays as fails.
Weekend gaps inflate delays → record the day of week and report weekday and weekend separately.
Oral option not stocked on the ward → check the formulary oral equivalents with pharmacy before the change goes live.
The EPMA prompt gets clicked through → audit the reason text in cycle 2, not just prompt completion.
pearls: Recruit an antimicrobial pharmacist; they already review IV lists daily.
Report IV days saved and cannulas avoided; managers respond to bed-days and line infections.
Use the national IVOS decision aid as the poster so wording matches the standard.
Hand the monthly IVOS report to the stewardship team so it outlives your rotation.

pitfalls: Local protocols use different sampling windows (e.g. 6–14 hours) → quote your Trust protocol in the report and keep it fixed between cycles.
Lab turnaround is the real delay at night → record sample and result times separately so ward and lab delays are not confused.
Doses delayed to wait for levels harm septic patients → count a dose held for a pending level as a pass only if documented.
EPMA build takes months → use a gentamicin chart sticker with a level time box in the interim.
Small numbers on one ward → pool courses across the hospital.
pearls: Recruit the antimicrobial pharmacist and a lab lead; both own part of the pathway.
Agree the exact protocol window with microbiology before cycle 1.
Record renal function too; it explains most high levels.
Ask pharmacy to run the report monthly after you rotate.

pitfalls: Phlebotomy rounds miss the pre-dose slot → agree that nurses take the level at dose time before cycle 1.
Dose times move after the first dose → record the actual next scheduled time, not the planned one.
Units move to continuous infusion mid-audit → exclude continuous infusions in both cycles.
The request fires but the sample is not labelled 'pre-dose' → add sample time to the lab request.
pearls: Recruit ward nurses early; they give the dose and can take the level.
Pair with the gentamicin audit to share one EPMA build.
Report days with an out-of-range level; it links timing to harm.
Leave the monthly search in the pharmacy TDM report.

pitfalls: Stated or estimated weights hide the error → record the weight source and report it.
Obese patients need capped doses → apply the guideline cap and do not count capped doses as fails.
ED gives the first dose before weighing → include ED doses and involve the ED pharmacist.
Calculator is bypassed with free text → check free-text orders in cycle 2.
pearls: Recruit ED and acute medicine; most first doses start there.
Put chair or bed scales where the first dose is given.
Agree the dose table with microbiology before cycle 1 so it does not change.
Pharmacist screening can keep the check alive after rotation.

pitfalls: No weight recorded → count as a fail; the clearance cannot be calculated.
Deliberate off-licence dosing by haematology → accept a documented specialist reason.
Creatinine changes during the stay → use the value nearest the first dose and keep that rule in both cycles.
Staff object to extra clicks → show how many patients were under- or over-dosed.
pearls: Recruit the anticoagulation pharmacist; they know the licence criteria by heart.
Report under-dosing as well as over-dosing; strokes persuade as much as bleeds.
Use one printed dose table for all four DOACs.
Build the check into pharmacy screening so it survives rotation.

pitfalls: Immobile patients cannot stand on scales → list where hoist or bed scales are kept before cycle 1.
ED gives the first dose before weighing → include ED starts and agree a weigh-in-ED rule.
Dose-banding tables differ between wards → use the single Trust table in both cycles.
Mandatory field filled with a guessed number → record the weight source in cycle 2.
pearls: Recruit a ward sister; nurses own the weighing.
Report how many doses were more than 10% off; it makes the risk concrete.
Link to the paracetamol weight audit; one weighing fix serves both.
Ask the thrombosis nurse to keep the monthly check.

pitfalls: Cards are given but not documented → accept a pharmacy counselling record as evidence.
Ambulatory patients leave without a discharge letter → include the ambulatory proforma as a data source.
Wards run out of cards → check stock on each ward before cycle 1.
Drug changes after discharge → record the drug at discharge only.
pearls: Recruit the thrombosis nurse and ward pharmacists; they already counsel.
Keep cards with the discharge medicines, not in an office.
Ask a few patients at follow-up if they still carry the card; it strengthens the report.
Leave the tick box report with the thrombosis team.

pitfalls: Duration is unclear from notes → use the GP record or drug history and keep the same rule in both cycles.
Short COPD courses are counted by mistake → exclude courses under 4 weeks unless repeated.
Staff assume the GP will issue it → agree with pharmacy that the card is given before discharge.
Cards run out → check ward and pharmacy stock before the change.
pearls: Recruit respiratory and rheumatology; they discharge most eligible patients.
Ask pharmacy to hand the card with the medicines at discharge.
Add inhaled high-dose steroids in a later cycle once oral is reliable.
Leave the EPMA report with the medication safety officer.

pitfalls: Steroid use missed at clerking → search EPMA for any steroid on the drug history as well as the chart.
Nurses record 'nil by mouth' and omit → include an IV/IM alternative on the prompt.
Deliberate stops look like omissions → accept a documented clinical decision.
EPMA delay codes are used loosely → agree what counts as an omission before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit acute medicine nursing leads; omissions happen on the first night.
Use the Trust omitted-doses report if one exists to find cases fast.
Tell one real near-miss story at the presentation; it changes practice.
Put the check into the ward pharmacist's daily screening.

pitfalls: Surgical patients follow a different pathway → keep to medical inpatients in both cycles, or audit surgery separately.
Nurses hold basal insulin when the patient is nil by mouth → include this in ward teaching and on the chart line.
Small numbers → extend the look-back period rather than mixing in DKA.
Prompt added but insulin not prescribed → check prescription and administration separately in cycle 2.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes specialist nurses; they see most VRIIIs.
Use the NaDIA harms data if your Trust submits it.
Record rebound hyperglycaemia after stopping; it shows the harm.
Hand the audit to the inpatient diabetes team for yearly repeat.

pitfalls: Fluid charts are incomplete → treat unrecorded periods as fails and agree this before cycle 1.
Fluid-overloaded patients need less volume → accept 10% glucose at a lower rate as a pass.
Pumps run out overnight → record gaps and their length, not just yes/no.
Order-set change needs IT time → use a printed combined chart in the interim.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes nurses and the IV fluids lead.
Check that the recommended bag is actually stocked on each ward.
Pair with the basal insulin audit; one data pull covers both.
Ask the diabetes team to repeat it yearly.

pitfalls: Pre-admission opioid use is unclear → check the GP record before counting as new.
Short supply implies a stop but no date is written → count only an explicit plan as a pass.
Surgeons object to extra fields → keep it to one mandatory line.
Mandatory fields are filled with 'as required' → review free text in cycle 2.
pearls: Recruit a surgical pharmacist and one consultant champion.
Share the result with the local primary care prescribing team; they see the downstream harm.
Record modified-release supplies; they are the highest risk.
Build the check into the pharmacy discharge screen so it outlasts the rotation.

pitfalls: Order sentences already include a maximum but are free-texted over → audit free-text orders separately.
Palliative teams object to caps → exclude end-of-life anticipatory prescriptions or allow a stated range.
Paper charts on some wards → include them and note the chart type.
Snapshot days miss weekend prescribing → collect across different days of the week.
pearls: Recruit the controlled drugs pharmacist; they run CD audits already.
Agree the order sentences with the acute pain team before the change.
Show one example where repeated doses caused sedation.
Leave the spot check with the CD accountable officer's team.

pitfalls: Pharmacy corrects errors silently → use the prescription as first submitted, not the dispensed version.
Gabapentinoids are missed as Schedule 3 → give auditors a schedule list.
IT cannot auto-generate words → use an EPMA pop-up reminder in the interim.
Different pharmacists record returns differently → agree the returned-prescription log fields first.
pearls: Recruit the dispensary lead; they keep the returns log.
Report discharge delay hours; bed managers will back the fix.
Add a one-slide example to FY1 induction.
Ask pharmacy to keep the monthly returns metric.

pitfalls: Letters say 'see drug chart' → count this as a fail; GPs cannot see it.
Allergy recorded in EPMA but not pulled through → check the IT mapping before cycle 1.
New allergies during admission are missed → record these separately; they matter most.
Specialties use different templates → sample across specialties in both cycles.
pearls: Recruit the EPR team early; the fix is an IT change.
Ask two local GPs how often letters lack allergies; quote them.
Record new in-hospital reactions as a sub-measure.
Hand the dashboard measure to the discharge quality lead.

pitfalls: Doctors' drug histories are counted as reconciliation → agree the definition (two sources, discrepancies addressed) before cycle 1.
Pharmacy managers see it as a staffing complaint → frame it as prioritising the highest-risk patients.
Timestamps are missing on paper → use EPMA only, or record time from notes consistently.
Bank holiday weekends skew data → note them and exclude or report separately.
pearls: Recruit the chief pharmacist early and share weekday data too.
Record critical medicines missed before reconciliation; that shows harm.
Use the Summary Care Record as a second source to speed it up.
Leave the weekend worklist report with the pharmacy duty manager.

pitfalls: Heart failure teams object to stopping → a documented reason to continue is a pass.
'Held' in notes but still given → check the administration record, not only the plan.
Sepsis diagnosis is vague → use the clerking diagnosis and keep the rule in both cycles.
Template line is ignored → check completion rate in cycle 2.
pearls: Recruit an acute physician and the AKI nurse.
Record AKI at 72 hours; even small differences make the case.
Keep the line short so it is filled in.
Ask the AKI team to repeat it yearly.

pitfalls: Product not recorded in the administration record → combine EPMA with ward stock and issue data.
Some wards need higher strength bags → agree a restricted list with pharmacy before cycle 1.
Concentrate reappears in stock after the audit → add it to the yearly stock check.
Staff fear running out of bags → confirm top-up levels with pharmacy.
pearls: Recruit the medication safety officer; this is a Never Event area.
Do the stock check with a ward pharmacist.
Report the stock check as a simple ward list.
Leave the yearly check with pharmacy.

pitfalls: Patients with no weight recorded are missed by the search → include blank weights and count them as fails.
Oral and IV doses are added together → record the total from all routes.
Elderly frail patients just over 50 kg are also at risk → note hepatotoxicity risk factors for later cycles.
Default dose rule is overridden → check overrides in cycle 2.
pearls: Recruit ward pharmacists; they catch most errors now.
Pair with the enoxaparin weight audit to share one weighing fix.
Show the SPS safety wording on one slide.
Leave the EPMA report with the medication safety officer.

pitfalls: The ARAF is signed in clinic but never reaches the practice → request a copy before counting a fail, and record 'requested' separately.
Small numbers in one practice → pool across the PCN and report counts as well as percentages.
A clinic letter that mentions the programme is counted as the form → count a pass only for the signed form or its scanned copy.
Specialists object that the ARAF is their job → frame the audit as the practice checking the safety net, not doing the specialist's review.
pearls: Recruit the PCN clinical pharmacist; valproate is already on their high-risk drug list.
Agree with the local neurology and mental health teams before cycle 1 that every ARAF is copied to the GP.
Code each form on receipt so the search finds it next time.
Hand the monthly register to the practice medicines lead so it survives the audit team's rotation.

pitfalls: Contraception fitted elsewhere (sexual health clinic) is not coded → check letters and ask the patient at recall before counting a fail.
Oral contraceptives are counted as highly effective → agree the list of highly effective methods before cycle 1 and keep it the same for the re-audit.
Topiramate is an enzyme inducer and can reduce hormonal contraceptive effect → flag this in the recall letter so the review covers method choice.
Patients feel accused by a letter about pregnancy → use neutral wording and the MHRA Patient Guide.
pearls: Recruit the practice's contraception lead nurse to run the recall clinic.
Use the MHRA Patient Guide and Risk Awareness Form so every review follows the same script.
Run the same search for valproate at the same time; the work is shared.
Put topiramate on the PCN high-risk drug list so the check survives rotation.

pitfalls: Bloods taken in hospital clinics are not visible in the GP record → check the shared results viewer before counting a fail.
Dermatology and gastroenterology intervals differ → record the specialty and use the SPS interval for each; keep the definition fixed for the re-audit.
Staff issue 'one more month' without bloods → the alert must show dates, not just a reminder.
The SPS entry is being updated to the 2025 BSR guideline → check the page before cycle 2 and keep the cycle 1 definition if it changes.
pearls: Recruit the practice's repeat prescribing clerks; they see every request first.
Agree with rheumatology which blood results they will copy to the practice.
Report the median days since the last FBC as well as the pass rate.
Hand the monthly search to the PCN pharmacist so it continues after the audit.

pitfalls: No recent weight, so creatinine clearance cannot be calculated → count 'cannot calculate' as a fail and fix it by adding weight to the AF review.
Auditors disagree on which body weight to use → agree actual body weight (or the local policy) before cycle 1 and keep it for cycle 2.
Deliberate off-label dosing by cardiology → record it as a documented exception, not a fail.
Clinicians change doses on one creatinine during an acute illness → use a stable result, not one taken during an admission.
pearls: Recruit the PCN pharmacist; DOAC reviews are a standard pharmacist task.
Use one online Cockcroft-Gault calculator for all auditors.
Report the number of patients on too high a dose; it is the figure that moves partners.
Link the template to the annual AF review so it runs without the audit team.

pitfalls: Cards given in hospital are never coded → check hospital letters and ask at the next contact before counting a fail.
Dose equivalents confuse the search → agree a conversion table (e.g. dexamethasone, hydrocortisone) before cycle 1.
The prompt is clicked through → count only coded issues, and show the override rate at the practice meeting.
Inhaled and topical steroid users are also eligible in some cases → keep this audit to oral steroids so the cycles stay comparable.
pearls: Recruit the dispensary or community pharmacy team; they can hand out cards when they supply prednisolone.
Order a stock of cards from NHS Forms before cycle 1.
Add card issue to the polymyalgia and COPD review templates, which cover most long-term users.
Name a medicines safety lead to own the prompt after the audit.

pitfalls: Injections given elsewhere (hospital or community nurses) are missing → check letters and ask the patient before counting a delay.
Small numbers in one practice → pool injections across the PCN.
The recall list is run once and then forgotten → put it on the nurse lead's monthly task list.
Blood tests delay the injection → agree that calcium is checked in the month before the due date, not on the day.
pearls: Recruit the practice nurse who gives most injections; she knows who is overdue.
Give every patient a card with their next due date.
Report the number of patients more than 7 months since their last dose; it shows the fracture risk plainly.
Share the results with the fracture liaison service, which may help fund recall.

pitfalls: A 7–14 day window is strict and patients test late → record the actual days and report 15–28 days separately.
Bloods taken by hospital clinics are not visible → check the shared results viewer.
Small numbers of new starters with CKD → widen to 6 months or pool across the PCN.
The booking task is created but ignored → give reception a weekly list of outstanding tasks.
pearls: Recruit the phlebotomy lead and reception manager; the fix is a booking step.
Agree with prescribers that the 'bloods in 10 days' task is part of the template, not optional.
Report any potassium above 6 found at follow-up; it makes the case.
Keep the protocol in the practice's prescribing policy so it survives staff changes.

pitfalls: One raised ACR during illness is counted → require a confirmed result as in NICE, and keep the rule for cycle 2.
Patients stopped the drug for good reasons that were never written down → count a documented reason as a pass and ask prescribers to record it.
Clinicians fear hyperkalaemia → pair the change with the 1–2 week blood check protocol.
Numbers are small in one practice → pool across the PCN.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes specialist nurse and the practice's diabetes GP lead.
Agree the ACR confirmation rule before cycle 1.
Show the list of untreated patients by name to the diabetes clinic team; it turns into action quickly.
Add the search to the existing diabetes recall so it runs after the audit.

pitfalls: Letters arrive days late → measure from the date the practice receives the letter as well as the discharge date.
Workflow staff miss asthma in long letters → include 'wheeze' and 'salbutamol' in the search terms and train the workflow team.
Parents do not answer calls → count two documented attempts as a separate category, not a pass.
Out-of-hours notifications are missed → include the out-of-hours system report in the case search.
pearls: Recruit the document workflow team; the fix happens at their desk.
Offer a telephone review; it is enough for the standard and easier to fit in.
Check inhaler technique and preventer adherence in the same call.
Share results with the local ED; faster letters help both sides.

pitfalls: Old, inactive registrants inflate the list → exclude patients with no asthma contact or issue in 2 years, and keep the rule for cycle 2.
Some people on the register do not have asthma → record diagnosis doubt as a reason rather than switching them.
Patients decline steroids → record informed decline, and report it separately.
Community pharmacy continues to supply old SABA repeats → update the repeat template, not just the formulary.
pearls: Recruit the practice asthma nurse and the PCN pharmacist.
Use the NICE/BTS/SIGN pathway diagram in every review so the message is the same.
Target people with 3 or more SABA inhalers first; they carry the most risk.
Add the search to the quarterly respiratory dashboard.

pitfalls: Spirometry access in the area is limited → record 'referred, awaiting test' separately so the audit shows the service gap.
Pre-bronchodilator results are counted → check the report and keep the definition for cycle 2.
Older adults with FEV1/FVC just above 0.7 are argued over → follow the NICE threshold and note borderline results.
Hospital diagnoses lack results in the record → request the report before counting a fail.
pearls: Recruit the practice's respiratory nurse and the local community spirometry hub.
Agree a 'suspected COPD' code for use while waiting for spirometry.
Report the number of patients on inhalers without a confirmed diagnosis.
Put the template in the practice coding policy so new staff use it.

pitfalls: Reviews by practice pharmacists or talking therapy workers are not coded as reviews → agree what counts before cycle 1 and search all staff groups.
Restarts are counted as new starters → require no antidepressant issue in the previous 12 months.
Patients do not answer the review call → record two documented attempts separately.
'Usually within 2 weeks' is read as optional → set the local target at 80%, not 100%.
pearls: Recruit the practice's mental health practitioner or care coordinator to run the calls.
Book the review before the patient leaves the first consultation.
A 14-day first supply builds the review in.
Hand the template to the practice mental health lead after the audit.

pitfalls: The clinic's capacity, not the practice, causes delay → record referral date so practice delay and service delay are shown separately.
Tests requested for other reasons (e.g. known heart failure) are counted → exclude known heart failure at the search stage.
Small numbers per practice → use the laboratory list for the whole PCN or locality.
The lab comment is ignored in busy result workflows → pair it with a pop-up in the results workflow.
pearls: Recruit the community heart failure nurse; they often run the one-stop clinic.
Ask the laboratory for the monthly list of results above 2,000 ng/L; it makes case finding easy.
Report the number admitted as an emergency before assessment; it makes the case for capacity.
Agree the pathway in writing with cardiology so it survives staff changes.

pitfalls: Uncoded presentations are missed → also search free text for 'PMB' and 'post-menopausal bleed'.
Bleeding on HRT is counted → record HRT use and exclude it, as NICE does.
Local pathways send patients straight to ultrasound → agree before cycle 1 which routes count as the suspected cancer pathway.
Patients who decline are counted as fails → record informed decline separately.
pearls: Recruit the practice cancer lead and the PCN cancer care coordinator.
Use the national referral form so criteria appear on screen.
Review every non-referred case at the practice cancer meeting; it is quick and educational.
Keep the pop-up in the practice's clinical system policy.

pitfalls: Haematuria is put down to anticoagulants → state in the template that anticoagulation does not explain it.
Presumed UTI without culture delays referral → record whether a culture was sent and the date.
Uncoded presentations are missed → search free text for 'blood in urine' and 'haematuria'.
Declined referrals are counted as fails → record them separately.
pearls: Recruit the practice cancer lead and a urology consultant to agree the template wording.
Report the median days from consultation to referral.
Discuss each non-referral at the cancer meeting; it teaches without blame.
Share the template across the PCN once it works.

pitfalls: Tests done for screening without symptoms are included → record symptoms and report asymptomatic tests separately.
Repeat PSA before referral is common local practice → agree before cycle 1 whether a repeat within 2 weeks counts, and keep it fixed.
Men over 79 inflate the list → NICE leaves them to clinical judgement; exclude them.
Filing by a clinician who did not request the test → record who filed it.
pearls: Recruit the practice cancer lead and the laboratory's duty biochemist.
Put the age thresholds on a card beside every screen.
Review every unactioned result at the monthly cancer meeting.
Make the results-workflow rule part of the practice's results protocol.

pitfalls: Radiology already books CT directly → record this and count it as a pass, but still check the patient was told.
Keyword searches miss unusual wording → agree the phrase list with a radiologist before cycle 1.
Small numbers → use a full year and the whole PCN.
Reports are filed by a locum who then leaves → the failsafe register must name the practice, not a person.
pearls: Recruit the radiology lead for GP reporting; they can add the alert code.
Treat any fail as a significant event and review it at the practice meeting.
Put the failsafe register on the shared practice drive with a named administrator.
Combine with the practice's other cancer failsafe checks to save time.

pitfalls: Clinicians say they explained but did not write it → the fix is a template field, not more teaching.
The tick-box is ticked by default → make it blank and mandatory.
Missed appointments have other causes → record them for interest, not as the pass criterion.
Clinicians worry about frightening patients → the NICE wording includes reassurance; build it into the template.
pearls: Recruit the PCN cancer care coordinator; they can phone patients after referral.
Link the national patient leaflet in the template.
Check availability for the next 2 weeks in the same step.
Keep the template in the practice's referral policy.

pitfalls: Re-authorisation is coded as a medication review → count a pass only when the note shows medicines were considered.
The eFI over-labels frailty → accept the coded list but record the frailty source.
Care home reviews by another team are not in the record → check care home pharmacist letters.
Pharmacist capacity runs out → prioritise those on 10 or more medicines.
pearls: Recruit the PCN clinical pharmacist; structured medication reviews are part of their role.
Agree what counts as a medication review before cycle 1.
Report the number of medicines stopped; it shows value.
Tie the search to the care home and frailty ward rounds so it continues.

pitfalls: Colposcopy letters are slow → wait 12 weeks before counting a fail, and check the hospital system.
Patients treated privately or elsewhere → record them and ask for letters.
The register is started and then dropped → name the administrator and a deputy.
Numbers are small → include the whole PCN and 12 months.
pearls: Recruit the practice's cervical screening administrator; they already receive results.
Agree with the colposcopy clinic that DNA letters are copied to the practice.
Treat any patient lost to follow-up as a significant event.
Combine with the sample-taker's 'every sample has a result' register for one failsafe routine.

pitfalls: Referral time missing for telephone referrals → log the time of the first call in the ENT referral book and use the same source in both cycles.
Small numbers make percentages jump → use a 12-month look-back first, re-audit prospectively over 6 months and report counts as well as percentages.
Conductive or middle ear causes included by mistake → confirm otoscopy and audiogram findings before counting a case.
Hot slot filled with routine cases → print the NG98 criteria on the booking form and let the ENT registrar veto misuse.
pearls: Recruit the audiology lead early: a same-day audiogram is usually the bottleneck.
Agree with the emergency department that out-of-hours cases get the next-morning slot, not a routine letter.
Put the pathway on the GP referral guidance page so it survives trainee rotation.

pitfalls: Parents object to four-times-daily liquid → offer the twice-daily regimen NG84 allows and explain it on the leaflet.
Pre-pack cupboard holds amoxicillin only → agree stock with pharmacy before cycle 1.
Unverified penicillin allergy labels → count clarithromycin as a pass only when an allergy is recorded; report the label rate separately.
Order set bypassed by free-text prescribing → check in week 6 how many prescriptions used it and remind the team.
pearls: Recruit the emergency department pharmacist; they own the pre-pack stock and the order set.
Agree the diagnosis codes to search with the coding team before cycle 1 and keep them the same.
Ask the stewardship team to report the measure quarterly so it outlives the audit team.

pitfalls: The form needs primary care agreement → take it through the cancer alliance or ICB clinical lead, not the hospital alone.
Scores ticked without real assessment → compare referral scores with the clinic findings in a sample of cases.
Referrals arrive by several routes → agree one extraction route before cycle 1 and keep it the same.
Worry that a low score will stop urgent referral → state on the form that clinical concern can still override the score.
pearls: Recruit a GP with a special interest in dermatology to champion the form.
Feed back each practice's scores and diagnoses; it motivates more than reminders.
Add a prompt to attach a dermoscopic photograph; it also supports teledermatology triage.

pitfalls: Stage not known at the time of the op note → take stage from the MDT outcome and record it before listing.
Margin written as 'WLE' without a number → make the numeric field required in the template.
Face and hand cases pull the rate down → count a documented reason for a reduced margin as a pass, as NICE allows.
Different surgeons read 'margin' differently → define it as the distance from the scar edge, agreed before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit one dermatologic surgeon and one plastic surgeon as joint leads so both services own it.
Ask the MDT coordinator to add the recommended margin to the MDT outcome letter.
Record the site; head and neck cases usually explain most variation.

pitfalls: Remote tests make dates unclear → record the date the test was done, not the date the result was uploaded.
Prescriptions are signed days before the clinic → define the prescription date as the date it is issued to the patient or pharmacy.
Childbearing status mislabelled → review the PPP status in every case, not only those on the PPP list.
Pharmacy pushback on refusing to dispense → agree the rule with the chief pharmacist before the change.
pearls: Recruit the dermatology specialist nurse who runs the PPP clinic; they hold the test log.
Align fields with the BAD national audit so one data set serves both.
Check homecare and community pharmacy prescriptions as well as hospital ones.

pitfalls: Start dates unknown when GPs started treatment → use the earliest prescription found and state the rule.
Eye service capacity objects to a surge of referrals → agree numbers and imaging slots with the medical retina lead before sending.
Patients monitored elsewhere are counted as fails → check community optometry or other trusts before scoring.
Lists miss patients on homecare or shared care → merge DMARD, homecare and pharmacy lists.
pearls: Recruit a rheumatology specialist nurse to own the monthly report.
Use a standard referral proforma with dose, weight, eGFR and tamoxifen use so the eye service can risk-stratify.
Include dermatology and lupus clinics, which are often missed.

pitfalls: Patients who did not attend are counted as service failures → record the reason and report both rates.
Requested interval not recorded → make the interval a required field on the outcome form.
Capacity limits make the target look impossible → pair the audit with a capacity-and-demand count so managers see the gap.
Tolerance changed between cycles → fix the 15% rule before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the outpatient booking lead and the service manager; they own the fix.
Present the number of patients now overdue, not only the percentage.
Use nurse-led or virtual glaucoma clinics for stable, low-risk patients to free consultant slots.

pitfalls: Checklist differs between wards → agree one hospital list with the tracheostomy lead before cycle 1.
Staff feel policed at the bedside → check with the nurse in charge and report by ward, not by name.
Very few patients on some days → spread checks across the fortnight and report counts.
Box emptied after use and not restocked → use numbered tags so an opened box is easy to spot.
pearls: Recruit critical care outreach; they see every ward tracheostomy and can issue the boxes.
Include laryngectomy patients; they are often on ENT or oncology wards without trache-trained staff.
Pair with the bedhead-sign check so one visit covers both.

pitfalls: Small numbers → use a 12-month look-back and report counts.
Reason given in the ward round note but not in the discharge summary → agree before cycle 1 which documents count and keep them fixed.
Staff see it as paperwork → show the NCEPOD ward-death findings when presenting cycle 1.
Field filled with 'as per plan' → define acceptable reasons in the template note.
pearls: Recruit the critical care tracheostomy lead and outreach team as co-leads.
Link the field to an automatic outreach referral so the ward gets support on day 1.
Record whether a cuff manometer was on the receiving ward; it often explains ward incidents.

pitfalls: Staff fear that asking implies blame → use neutral wording in the box and explain it is asked of every child.
Checklist in paper notes gets lost → build it into the electronic template.
Paediatric liaison already reviews cases → agree that their note does not count unless it is made during the attendance.
Changing the age range between cycles → fix under 5 before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the named safeguarding nurse or doctor as co-lead.
Use the child's development stage (mobility) prompt; it catches most non-mobile scalds.
Include urgent treatment centres, where many small scalds are seen.

pitfalls: Pre-hospital cooling not written down → ask about it at triage and record 'unknown' rather than guessing.
Children get cold → cool the burn and keep the child warm, as the guidance says; exclude large burns.
Busy triage skips cooling → make the sink location and a timer part of the triage step.
Hydrogel used instead of water → record it separately; it does not count as cooling.
pearls: Recruit the triage nurse lead; they own the template.
Put a clock and a laminated '20 minutes' sign above the designated sink.
Share results with the ambulance service; they can change the handover template too.

pitfalls: pH strips not stocked → check stock before cycle 1 and add them to the pack list.
Patient leaves or moves to eye casualty before the 30-minute check → allow the eye unit's documented check to count.
Small numbers → use a 12-month look-back and report counts.
Staff unsure what 'normal' is → print the target pH range on the sticker.
pearls: Recruit an emergency nurse practitioner who sees most minor eye injuries.
Keep the pack sealed and tagged so used packs are easy to spot and restock.
Include industrial and cleaning-product injuries from occupational health reports to find cases.

pitfalls: Advice given but not written down → make the tick-box part of the discharge template, not free text.
Leaflet not stocked → print it from the template instead of relying on paper stock.
Children seen again in dressing clinic are double-counted → count the first discharge only.
Parents with limited English → include translated or pictorial versions of the leaflet.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric emergency nurse lead and the burns outreach nurse.
Ask the burns unit to check advice was given at their follow-up call.
Keep the advice short: fever, rash, diarrhoea or vomiting, drowsiness, return straight away.

pitfalls: Swollen lids make examination hard → allow a documented reason plus ophthalmology review to count as a pass.
Equipment kept only in the eye room → stock strips and a blue light in the burns bay.
Face shaded on the body map but not coded as facial burn → search the body map as well as diagnosis codes.
Intubated patients missed → include them; eye checks matter most when patients cannot report symptoms.
pearls: Recruit an ophthalmology registrar to give a 10-minute demonstration at the start.
Link the fluorescein field to the facial burn leaflet so both are done together.
Report corneal injuries found; they persuade staff more than percentages.

pitfalls: Few cases each year → use a 24-month look-back if needed and report counts.
'Senior' means different grades → fix the definition before cycle 1 and keep it.
Anaesthetist review happens but is written only on the anaesthetic chart → search both records.
Burn team asks for a review only when stridor appears → the trigger must use the full feature list, not stridor alone.
pearls: Recruit an anaesthetic consultant as co-lead; they can change the call criteria.
Measure carboxyhaemoglobin in every enclosed-space fire; it helps identify cases.
Share each case in joint emergency and anaesthetic morbidity meetings.

pitfalls: INR from the anticoagulation clinic has no time → record date and time from the pathology system or meter log.
Stability is unknown → count as unstable unless the anticoagulation record shows otherwise.
Meter quality control lapses → assign one named nurse and follow the manufacturer's checks.
Patients told by others to stop warfarin → record interruptions separately; they are a harm too.
pearls: Recruit the clinic nurse lead, who will run the meter.
Send patients the SDCEP warfarin instruction sheet with their appointment letter.
Agree with the anticoagulation clinic how to share recent INR results.

pitfalls: Edentulous patients skipped → include them; dentures and bone still need checking.
Assessment done at another hospital → accept any specialist dental record if it is in the notes before radiotherapy.
Fast-tracked treatment starts before dental review → flag these at MDT and record the reason.
Dental team capacity → agree a ring-fenced weekly slot for MDT referrals before the change.
pearls: Recruit the restorative dentistry consultant who sits on the MDT.
Ask the MDT coordinator to add dental status to the MDT outcome letter.
Record days from extraction to radiotherapy too; it shows whether the pathway is early enough.

pitfalls: No headlight or silver nitrate available → stock the trolley before cycle 1 and check it daily.
Doctors unsure how to cauterise → pair the trolley with a short hands-on session from ENT.
Posterior bleeds counted as failures → accept 'no bleeding point seen' as a pass when examination is documented.
ENT and emergency department disagree on who treats first → agree the pathway jointly before the change.
pearls: Recruit an ENT registrar and an emergency department nurse practitioner as joint leads.
Report packs and admissions avoided; managers care about bed days.
Keep the pathway on the trolley itself so it survives staff rotation.

pitfalls: Paper proformas are ignored → build the field into the electronic triage screen instead.
No chart or pinhole at triage → install both before cycle 1.
Near-vision cards used without recording → accept any recorded method but note which.
Busy periods lead to 'not done' → allow a documented reason, then track how often it is used.
pearls: Recruit the triage nurse lead and the IT template owner early.
Mark the floor at the correct distance for the chart; it removes an excuse.
Share one missed diagnosis case at the start; it convinces staff.

pitfalls: Target written only on the biometry printout → agree before cycle 1 which records count.
Surgeons assume 'distance' by default → the field should force an explicit choice.
Second-eye surgery copies the first-eye target without discussion → count each eye separately.
Independent-sector records not accessible → limit the sample to in-house lists.
pearls: Recruit the cataract lead nurse or optometrist who runs pre-assessment.
Link the field to the lens-ordering step so it cannot be skipped.
Audit the second eye separately if numbers allow; errors cluster there.

pitfalls: Score calculated but written only in the endoscopy request → search ED notes, clerking and the request, and count it only if it is timed before the disposition decision.
ED staff see the score as the medical team's job → agree before cycle 1 which team owns it (usually the first clinician) and put that on the proforma.
Missing urea or haemoglobin at first assessment → allow a score recorded once the first bloods return, and note the time.
Small numbers of score-0 patients → report score-0 discharges as context only, not as a pass criterion.
Gains fade when the proforma is bypassed → track use of the proforma alongside the pass rate.
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant and a gastroenterologist as joint sponsors before cycle 1.
Build the calculator so it fills from the observations and blood results already in the EPR; manual scoring is where it fails.
Ask the endoscopy booking team to return requests without a score: this keeps the change alive after the audit team rotates.
Feed back monthly run charts to the ED huddle for the first 3 months.

pitfalls: Suspected variceal bleed is judged after the event → define 'suspected' before cycle 1 as known cirrhosis, portal hypertension or stigmata of chronic liver disease in the clerking.
Drug given in endoscopy is recorded late → use the endoscopy start time from the endoscopy system and the administration time on the drug chart, not the prescription time.
Small numbers → extend the look-back window rather than dropping below 30 cases, and keep the same window length in cycle 2.
Pharmacy objects to ED stock because of cost → show the cost of one extra ITU day; agree a small stock with expiry checks.
pearls: Recruit a hepatology consultant and the ED pharmacist before cycle 1.
Pair terlipressin with antibiotics in one order set so both happen together.
Put a laminated 'suspected variceal bleed' action card on the ED resus wall.
Ask endoscopy nurses to check terlipressin status at the pre-procedure safety pause.

pitfalls: Primary-prevention aspirin mixed in → record the indication from medicines reconciliation and exclude primary prevention.
Clinicians fear rebleeding → record rebleeding as a safety measure and share it with the endoscopists.
Haemostasis time unclear → agree before cycle 1 that the endoscopy report or first 'no further bleeding' note is the time point.
Aspirin restarted in hospital but dropped from the discharge letter → check both the inpatient chart and the discharge prescription.
pearls: Recruit the endoscopy lead and a ward pharmacist.
Put the prompt where the decision is made: the endoscopy report.
Share the rebleeding data; it usually reassures sceptical colleagues.
Ask pharmacists to flag stopped secondary-prevention aspirin at discharge screening.

pitfalls: Prescribed but not given → count administration time, not prescription time.
Eligibility unclear from notes → agree the malnourishment definition (MUST ≥1 or intake poor) before cycle 1 and keep it for cycle 2.
Pharmacy supply delays on wards → check ward stock of Pabrinex before cycle 1.
Order set used for everyone, including low-risk drinkers → report total use as a balancing measure.
pearls: Recruit the alcohol care team nurse as co-lead; they already track these patients.
Link the order set to the alcohol question in the clerking so it fires automatically.
Put Pabrinex in the acute medical unit and ED stock lists.
Re-brief each new FY1 intake at induction with a one-slide reminder.

pitfalls: Nurses unfamiliar with scoring → train ward nursing leads before the change, not doctors alone.
Fixed regimens still appropriate for some (e.g. history of seizures) → allow 'fixed with documented reason' as a separate category and report it.
Scores recorded on paper and not in EPR → agree before cycle 1 where scores are found and search both.
Over-sedation fears → track total benzodiazepine dose and sedation events as balancing measures.
pearls: Make the alcohol care team and a ward matron co-owners.
Choose one tool (CIWA-Ar or GMAWS) Trust-wide and keep it.
Put the score-to-dose table on the chart itself.
Show the drop in total benzodiazepine dose; it wins over sceptical staff.

pitfalls: Taps done in ED not linked to the admission → search laboratory records by patient number from the ED arrival time.
Ascites too small to tap → record ultrasound findings and exclude only when documented.
Clinicians worry about bleeding with a high INR → share the BSG advice that routine clotting checks and blood products are not needed before paracentesis.
Weekend admissions dominate failures → report weekday and weekend results separately.
pearls: Recruit a hepatology consultant and the acute medicine lead.
Keep ascitic tap packs and blood-culture bottles on the acute medical unit.
Offer a short supervised tap session for resident doctors in the first month.
Make the bundle the default admission document for anyone coded with decompensated cirrhosis.

pitfalls: Volume drained not recorded when the drain is removed → make total volume a required field in the procedure record.
Albumin given in 100 ml bottles makes exact dosing impossible → allow ±10% and round to whole bottles.
Albumin given for drains under 5 L (in ACLF or high renal risk) → record separately; BSG allows it in these cases.
Blood bank issues recorded but not given → use the administration record, not issue data.
pearls: Recruit the day unit sister; they own the procedure record.
Pre-print the dose table on the drain chart.
Involve the transfusion practitioner; albumin usage data are already collected.
Show the cost saved, not only compliance, at the transfusion committee.

pitfalls: 'No cause identified' is judged in hindsight → decide eligibility from notes written in the first 24 hours only.
Radiology pushes back on extra urgent scans → show the numbers (usually 2–5 a week) and agree the slot in advance.
Scans requested but not done at weekends → report weekday and weekend separately.
Over-requesting when the cause is clear (NICE 1.4.4) → track scans in patients with a clear cause as a balancing measure.
pearls: Recruit a nephrologist and an ultrasound lead radiographer before cycle 1.
Use the laboratory AKI alert list; it gives every case with a time stamp.
Put the NICE wording in the RIS request option so vetting radiologists accept it.
Include catheter status; a bladder scan may answer the question first.
